projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Maynard Wesley Unger was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: This is the oral history of World War II veteran Maynard Wesley Unger, known as "Doc." Mr. Unger served in the U.S. Army Air Corps with the 381st Bomb Group. Doc served in the European Theater, and his highest rank was Tech Sergeant. I'm Tom Swope, and this recording was made at Mr. Unger's home in Lakewood, Ohio, on October 23rd, 2003. Doc was 82 at the time of this recording. Where were you living in 1941?

sp.speaker: Maynard Wesley Unger
sp.p: I was living in Oberlin, Ohio, on East College Street, and --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How old were you --

sp.speaker: Maynard Wesley Unger
sp.p: -- and I lived with my parents. I was 20 years old.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: -- in 1941? Were you working or in school?

sp.speaker: Maynard Wesley Unger
sp.p: I was working. And for whatever reason, another fellow and I decided that we were gonna join the army. And the day came when we were going to leave, and a high school friend of mine, who is still a friend today, came over to pick me up. He lived in Elyria and drove me to Elyria, where this other fella lived. His name was Dick Robson. And before we ever got out of the car, his mother was at the door and said: "Richard is not going to the army." And that left me high and dry all alone, but my friend -- his name was Hal Frederick -- drove me into Cleveland to the recruiting station, and I enlisted there. And this was in October of '41, and they put me on a bus and sent me to Columbus, Fort Hayes, and I was actually sworn in at Fort Hayes. And --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What can you tell me about your training?

sp.speaker: Maynard Wesley Unger
sp.p: Well, after -- from Fort Hayes, I took my basic training to Ellington Field, Texas, and this was a big thing then. It's a long trip. They give you these Pullman tickets and you eat in the dining room, and we lived pretty lavishly going down. And there weren't too many people that took basic training in, in -- at Ellington Field, Texas. That's in the Houston area. And I was in what they called a feather merchant platoon, all the little guys.

And it was pretty rugged. I can remember standing inspections, and I have a recollection of a big, tall, handsome guy standing outside in the hallway in front of the room and he just fainted. He was, apparently he just was so erect and so immobile that he fainted. This same fella shows up later on in my record because he ended up in the same outfit that I did.

It rained a lot when we were in basic training. Certainly we did a lot of marching -- march, march, march. I told my wife -- and I had this confirmed with a fellow that was in the same platoon -- that it rained so hard the water was knee deep and they still made us march to the mess hall. And I, I never gave up or anything, but it -- you, you learn a lot of things in those first few weeks.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you choose the Army Air Corps in the beginning?

sp.speaker: Maynard Wesley Unger
sp.p: Yeah. When I -- they give you the aptitude tests, and because of my score, I had a choice. I could go into the army or I could go into the Air Corps, and I always wanted to fly and so I chose the Air Corps.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So were you still there on December 7th, 1941?

sp.speaker: Maynard Wesley Unger
sp.p: No. I finished my basic training. And actually, I was -- my first base assignment was in Bangor, Maine, so here again, we're back on a train going to Bangor, Maine. On December 7th, another fellow and I that was also in this platoon that I was in in basic were at a movie in Bangor on that Sunday, and when we came out of the movie there was an air policeman that gathered us up and told us we had to get back to the base.

I don't remember exactly what his words were but it was an emergency of some sort. And he stopped the first car that came by and ordered them to drive us out to the air base, which was right on the outskirts of town. And then from then on, why, we were kinda bound to the base for a long time till they could figure out what was going on.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was your reaction to that news when you heard it?

sp.speaker: Maynard Wesley Unger
sp.p: Well, I wrote a letter on December 7th to my grandmother, and it must have been before Roosevelt made his speech, because I said: "It looks like we're going to be in a war and that, don't worry. I still hoped to get home on my furlough for Christmas and so forth." I didn't, but I did mention the word "war" but I don't think it was actually declared yet then. And --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Anything else from your training time that comes to mind?

sp.speaker: Maynard Wesley Unger
sp.p: Well, I remember once we went on a, a pass, and it must have been on Veterans Day and we were downtown and we were standing on a kind of a marquee of a hotel watching the parade go by, and it had to have been Veterans Day. That was in downtown Houston.

I made some good friends, one that -- well, he's dead now but he lived from Ohio. He didn't enlist with me. We shared the same birthday, and our serial numbers were only a couple numbers apart. And one, one of the fellas that was our instructor when we were in basic training -- his name was Archie Baldo Gonzales (ph) -- happened to be assigned to Bangor, Maine, when we were assigned there and we used to pick on him all the time.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was your job then?

sp.speaker: Maynard Wesley Unger
sp.p: At that time I was a -- when I say a mechanic, I was an assigned to the flight line and helping them to repair airplanes. And the only thing that I can really remember -- I'm a small person, and there was a problem on the wing of this B-18 airplane, and they put me up through this hole into the wing to do something, and I don't remember what it was but because of my size, I know I was the one to do it.

The -- when, when war broke out, we were in, in Bangor, Maine. We, we had assignments we had runway guard duty. They put people on the runways. Two people were assigned with a truck. One person could set in the truck, run the truck and run the heater, and the other person would walk the runway. And then when he got cold, he'd get back in the cab of the truck and the other person would walk.
I don't -- I think that, I just had the feeling that they didn't know what was going to happen. They were just try to take every precaution.

One of the duties was to guard where the, the Norton bomb site, just a little caged-in area. And another one of the duties that you got was to stoke the fires. The barracks were all furnaces or coal-fired furnaces, and if you had that duty, you had to keep that going. Basically those were the, the three jobs -- well, KP, of course. Everybody had a turn at KP. And it gets a lot of play but it's, it's not as bad as people make it sound.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You kind of enjoyed it at times?

sp.speaker: Maynard Wesley Unger
sp.p: And while, while I was in Bangor, Maine, I had applied to go to flight school. As I've indicated earlier, I really wanted to fly, and I thought I was all set to go and they found something wrong with my eye. And then there's an opportunity to go to gunnery school, and I don't know whether I volunteered or was picked, but I went to gunnery school -- and remember, the war started December 7th. New Year's Eve I was back out west.

I was in Las Vegas, Nevada, aerial gunnery school. And so we had those great train rides back and forth. And so I trained -- I'm not sure whether it was four weeks or six weeks -- to be an aerial gunner, and then we went back to Bangor, Maine, and again on those beautiful train rides. And one of the interesting things that happened, there were five of us that were at gunnery school at that time, and we had laid around for quite awhile because our original outfit had been transferred oversees. And we all lived reasonably close to towns and reasonably close to the railroad. And we decided that as for -- in my case when it comes through Cleveland I would get off, stay home 24 hours, get back on the same train the next day, and people subsequent along the way would do the same.

By the time we left New York, everybody was back together again, and we all checked in at the same time so we were actually AWOL but nobody knew it. And so then we were assigned to the, the squadron that was there, 92nd Reconnaissance Squadron, and our job was to do coast line patrol. At that time there were just -- the submarines were playing havoc with the merchant ships that were trying to get goods across to England and so forth, and our job was to look for submarines.

And we flew in A-29s, which is a Lockheed Hudson twin tail with an open cockpit in the back like a, a, a reversible rumble seat in a sense. And I was a, an observer, and I rode in the, in the back. And those were our missions. And we followed the, the submarines as the danger would increase at various places. And I went from Bangor, Maine, TDY to Mitchell Field, New York. And while we were there, our whole outfit moved to Mitchell Field, New York. And we lived in one of the hangars -- this big hangar with all of these bunks in it.

And all of your activity -- I remember we played a lot of cards, and of course back then, maybe they still do -- had a lot of gambling. You're playing cards and rolling dice and doing almost anything for entertainment. Still flying. I remember asking our bombardiers -- we had enlisted bombardiers -- and I said: "Can these airplanes fly on one engine?" And he said: "Well, I assume they can." He said: "I don't know."

The very next time we went out, we had a, an engine failure and they brought it back to the base with one engine. And the fire trucks were down there and it was really a scary situation but it was just as nice a landing as you could have.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you ever spot any submarines when you were out there on patrol?

sp.speaker: Maynard Wesley Unger
sp.p: We did just once that I -- well, I think that we thought that we spotted 'em, but we only once dropped depth charges. Our, our, our Reconnaissance Squadron did get credit for, for a couple submarines but none that I was flying on. But we followed them from Mitchell Field, New York, to Langley Field, Virginia, Opa-Laka Naval Air Station, which is in Miami, from Miami to Mobile, Alabama, and Mobile, Alabama, to Galveston, Texas. Those were all places that I was stationed in.

And I'd only been in the service about a year. In Galveston, Texas, we were a little civilian airport, and orders came out that you now had to go to two technical schools, so I suppose based on my aptitude tests, when it came in, one of the, my friends in this feather merchant platoon was still with me. We were sent to radio school in Salt Lake City.

And it came easy to me, not so for my friend. His name was Buss Beeson. And I did my best to try to keep him in school. We set next to each other, would reach around, but he eventually washed out and then I didn't see him anymore. And I finished radio school and got promoted, I think maybe promoted, I'm not sure whether it was buck sergeant or staff sergeant. Staff sergeant, I think. Went to Blythe, California, and was assigned to an air crew, and we did a little bit of training there, but then we were transferred to Texas and formed 381st Bomb Group.
And we were the first bomb group on that particular air base. And most of us lived in tents, and it was dusty. You had to wear dust masks when you were down around the flight line all the time at --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What --

sp.speaker: Maynard Wesley Unger
sp.p: -- that -- go ahead.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I was just gonna ask: What kind of planes were you flying at that time?

sp.speaker: Maynard Wesley Unger
sp.p: Well, on B-17s.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: B-17s? All right.

sp.speaker: Maynard Wesley Unger
sp.p: It was a B-17E. And we were -- when we went up, and I often remarked that the first time I went up in a B-17, this was, we were still in California, and the, the transmitter, you had to tune it, and you had an antenna that was a trailing that you let it out so far and, and I guess the only way I could reach the ground would have been with a rock.

I just could not get through to anybody. And eventually, why, that -- but then we, we went to Pyote (ph), Texas, and formed the bomb group. And we trained out of Pyote, Texas, for several, several months.

The only change to my crew, the tail gunner was a, a man by the name of Zach, and he had had an ear infection or mastoid, but they assigned a new person to our plane as a tail gunner. And those are the same people I flew with all the time. And we trained and trained, and trained. Flying, practicing formation, landings and take-offs and bomb runs. One of the times -- I'm not sure whether it was out of that base -- but in one of our trainings, we, we dropped leaflets in San Diego, I think it was. They were war bonds, buy war bonds, but in a sense a practice run.

We went from Texas to Salina, Kansas, Pueblo, Colorado. We picked up a brand new airplane, which was a B-17F, and we trained a little bit more, got familiar with the plane, and then our Bomb Group was ready to go overseas. And we went over in May of 1943, and those of us that were on the air crews flew over. We flew our own airplane over.

And when we were in Selfridge (ph) Field, we had some motor trouble, delayed us a few days. I always suspicioned that it was faked because I know that the pilot's wife showed up at Selfridge Field and visited a little bit with the people. And then we went to Bangor, Maine. And I think the only -- and the same base where I trained, Dow Air Force Base. That used to be Bangor Air Force Base. The nose art was put on our airplane.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was she called?

sp.speaker: Maynard Wesley Unger
sp.p: Hell's Angels.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Maynard Wesley Unger
sp.p: And I don't know whose idea that was. Somebody at the base. That was their job to try to get you going. Then we flew to Gander, Newfoundland and we got weathered in there for a while. It was really cold, a lot of snow at that time even. And then we went from there to Prestrie, Scotland; Prestrie, Scotland, to our air base.

And it was a whole new thing when you go over there for a radio person. They got these balloon barrages in the sky, and we, we trained with Q signals. They had Z signals and -- but the radio job was important but it wasn't as important when you -- one radioman was most important when you were on a mission. And so a brand new thing for everybody. The day we flew -- I was gonna say our first mission -- but it was before I flew. I did not fly on the first mission of, of our bomb group. Everybody doesn't fly. The, the second day a bomb exploded and killed 26 people on the flight line. Some of the air crew, ground people, some civilians. And nonetheless we still flew a mission on that day. That was my first mission.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you ever find out was it just a faulty bomb or --

sp.speaker: Maynard Wesley Unger
sp.p: I don't, I don't know. I don't know. But it was really a scary thing, and I don't know whether it got -- they're generally pretty safe. They've got a, a pin that you have to pull to -- but something happened. It was --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So what are the memories of your first mission?

sp.speaker: Maynard Wesley Unger
sp.p: I don't think I ever went on any mission that I wasn't scared. And, of course, I, I think there was a good deal of apprehension because of that disaster on the ground before we left. A fellow radioman was killed on the first mission. The plane came back, but he'd gotten a stray bullet or something. And I, I've rationalized a lot about this. I, I -- we were pretty cocky. If something was gonna happen, it was gonna happen to the other guy.

And the first mission, as I recall, was not really bad. You, you never went on a mission that you didn't encounter some kind of flak or fighters or -- there was always something. But sometimes it was lighter than others or they picked on another group of airplanes, you know.

The, the airplanes flew as a group. I think we probably have maybe 26 to 32 planes in a bomb group, and they'd stack them up different levels and they followed each other. And if you were the low element, that's where you get the most, so you never wanted to fly the, the low element. But I, I've -- I, I know I was always scared but what, what made it worthwhile, I think, when you come back from a mission, we were a team, and everybody on the base would come back, they know that, say, 24 airplanes left, and they'd count the airplanes and then they don't get the right number and then sometimes it would be one is way behind still coming or indeed shot down.

But in the radio, there's an open hatch on top of the plane, and the enlisted men, of which there would be five of us, there were six enlisted men but the engineer was up front but everybody else, we -- they'd get up and sit around this open area, and we were treated like we just won the world series, you know.

People raise and cheer and we were big heros. And I think that buoyed to, to want to keep going. And what we did have -- I, I ended up flying 12 missions successfully. I got shot down on my 13th. At the end of the 12 -- I don't know whether it was 12 -- but our crew had a pass.

And we went to London, so I did get to see a little bit of London and the big USO place there. I don't know where we stayed overnight, but it was just a weekend. And ironically, when I got back I wrote my grandmother, one of my grandmothers, that I'd been on pass and that everything was going -- you couldn't tell 'em exactly what you were doing. I mentioned that I had received the air medal -- and you get this for a certain number of missions, so they knew that you were flying missions. And that it appeared that everything's going well. I expected to get this war over and be home by Christmas. And it was the very next mission that I got shot down on.

We used to go into town. We did some volunteer work while we were there. You know, you don't fly every day. You don't know when you're going to fly. That's the thing about it. You, you're going along fine and then all of a sudden three o'clock in the morning they wake you up and say: "Come on. You gotta go." So you never knew. That, of course, was for safety purposes.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Maynard Wesley Unger
sp.p: But we did some volunteer work at a, an orphanage I know I mentioned in one of my letters home. A lot of this stuff I don't remember clearly. I remember the orphanage. But I mentioned that when I was on pass, I said I used to play golf. She said I played golf the other day. I don't remember playing golf. I remember -- and I said -- we went boating. I remember going boating.

And we were in this park and one of the waist gunners was probably the one that I spent most time with. He and I were trying to flirt with these girls. We had a canoe and I fell out of canoe, got, got wet, and we must have had to take a taxi to some laundry someplace. They dried my clothes out. And -- but that was the only time that we were in London.

But we used to go locally to the local pubs, ride our bicycles. And I know that just shortly before I got shot down, I bought a brand new bicycle, and the little pub, watching the British play darts and --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you get along with the British people?

sp.speaker: Maynard Wesley Unger
sp.p: Yeah. Yeah. We -- and some lady did our laundry for us. We hired the laundry done. I think we took it up there and dropped it off and then picked it up. When I say "us," I don't know how many. We lived in Quonset huts, and there were ten people in a Quonset hut and there were ten people in a Quoset hut -- I'm counting right. Must have been six people -- tail gunner, two waist gunners, ball turret, radio and engineer. Six enlisted and four officers. So there were in the hut so -- and our squadron was all together.

And I remember they, those are corrugated, those huts, and our, our ball turret gunner used to get soused up every once in a while, and he ran around with a guy on another crew that was in our same little hut. And one night I remember a, a gun went off and somebody said that must have been Savagey (ph). He said he was gonna fire his gun sometime.

But these guys come home and they park their bicycle along the hut and it would go (unreportable noise) handlebars running along the side. They had a movie on the base, and entertainment. We weren't lacking for things to do.
We had our own individual mess hall for the flight people, I suppose because of the odd hours that, that we were in compared to the ground people. So we were, we were, we were kind of cocky people.

We, we thought we were special. And the, the people -- and the day I got shot down was the first Schweinford (ph) mission, which was August 17th, 1943. And it was delayed for, I don't remember all these hours, but as long as five hours before we got off the ground. It was a big adventure. Some people were gonna leave England, hit the target in Regansburg (ph), and go to Africa. And some were coming from Africa to Regansburg and come back. And most of us were going.

That was a diversion. We were going to Schweinert. They lost over 50 planes on that day, and in our squadron we lost four planes, and the, the 24 people that got shot down were -- well, I don't know where the officers' quarters were, but nobody came back from either one of those two huts.
And, of course, whatever you had, your personal belongings were shipped home but that's all. I always wondered who got that nice new bicycle.

And our particular plane never got to the target. A plane -- we were, we had lost one engine but we were still in formation and a plane got hit in the element above us, came down through our formation, and the pilot had to move out of the formation to avoid an air collision, and his plan was to circle around and maybe get with another group.

And I've never been -- in all the flying I did, never been in an airplane that really he had it in such a tight bank, it just, (unreportable noise) just -- and we couldn't make it to there. And of course out there then the fighters were like a beehive on us and, and hitting the plane, the plane got on fire, another, an engine got on fire, and the pilot sent the word out to abandon the plane.

And I know I looked up through the bomb bay. We had, we still had our bombs. And I looked up through the bomb bay, and the engineer was there and he was, you know -- I'm, you're the radioman. Engineer was motioning to get out, but they dropped the bombs. And then that left the bomb bay open. That door was open during a mission.

And so I'm, I'm scared to death. I, I really make no bones about that. I thought the plane was gonna blow up any minute. It didn't. A radio person, I did not wear my parachute. I had a snap-on chest pack, so I picked it up and snapped it on, and I tried to get out into the bomb bay and I couldn't go. I hadn't disconnected my oxygen mask. I hadn't disconnected my headset, so in near panic I'm back in there. Finally got them off, and I went out of the airplane rear end first.

And from then on it was kind of like a tape recorder. One of the things that happens in the military, you are trained. We had practiced getting out of the airplane. We never parachuted but we knew where we were gonna go out. We practiced that on the ground. We practiced ditching the airplane in the channel. We knew where the life rafts were. Everybody had jobs to do. So it's almost like all of that coming back.

And so I knew I had to get free of the airplane, and I was free of the airplane. And then this little tape recorder was saying: Fall as far as you can without, you know, they'd get you out of the flak, get you down to where there's less danger, that they would try to shoot you in a parachute.

So I'm falling, and I'm looking and next thing when the ground starts coming up fast, that's when you should pull your chute and it looked to me like it was coming up pretty fast. I pulled the chute, and it went open and it, you know, going, I don't know, free fall, what, near 90 some miles an hour, I guess. And all of that air rushing by it's almost dead silence.

And I think for a moment I thought I was dead. But then I could here the guns still going off in the distance, and I was very close to the ground. I landed in the backyard in a little, little village. And while I was on the ground, a plane crashed in the hillside over there. I don't know whether that was ours or not. I, I didn't get a good -- I don't even know if it was a B-17.

But then this tape recorder's saying: You gotta get out of your parachute. Fold it up. Hide it. Before I ever got it untangled, there was a guy there with a gun on me. And I couldn't understand what he was saying, but I knew what he meant, and I put my hands up. He had me gather up all my stuff, made me carry it myself. And we wore heated suits. And I always wore mine on the outside of my flight coveralls. And it was a, a baby blue. They're bright, and they got wires all over 'em. And this is what I was wearing. This was in August. It was a hot day.

And we had to walk quite a distance, and I finally convinced him somehow that I needed to get out of that suit. He let me get out of the suit but I had to carry it too. And the shoes were the, the electric heated boots. They're just a soft thing with wires in 'em and -- but it was tough going. They took me to a car, and there, there was a young fella, a young kid probably 15, 16 years old with him.

This fella's, I've learned since, was an air raid warden. And they drove me to a little village. And I'm sitting in the back of this car and they're parked and the kid is still there. He's got a gun. And the villagers all come out to get a look at this Americano. He went in, I assume, to make a phone call. And I remember two girls standing very close to the car looking down there, snickering at me. And I felt about that -- not very big. And I'm, I'm scared. You, you -- no bravo here.

And he came out. Apparently he was told to take us to the town of Wiesbaden. Now, I know now that I have spent -- after my 22 months in captivity, I have spent six years of my life back in Germany so I know a lot more.

But it turned out to be Wiesbaden at the Kerr Haus, which is like our city hall or -- and a big stately building with marble walls and floors and people are walking around clicking their heels -- "Heil Hitler. Heil Hitler." Seemed like every time they turned a corner they -- "Heil Hitler." And I -- at this point I'm not carrying my chute as I recall. I don't know what happened to that. Probably stayed in the car. And they took me in and there was a fellow that talked, he had broken English but he spoke good English with an accent, I should say, and they put me in a storage room of an office. There was a table and a chair.

And they questioned me. And of course training -- name, rank and serial number. I'm scared to death. And they, they wanted to be nice to me. They tried to bring some soup to me and that. I would have nothing to do with it. I didn't know whether I thought they were going to poison me. I really don't know. And this one -- and he came in every, people came in every once in awhile. Time wise, I don't know exactly how long I was there. Probably two or three hours.

And then finally they came and there were two military people, and they took me and marched me out through this hall again. I don't recall if they had their guns drawn or anything but it was still all this "Heil Hitler" put me in a touring car. And we watched a lot of movies years ago and they had these big, long, like a long convertible, a driver and a guy with a guard up front with a gun and there was another guard. There were three guards now. There was one in the car. He sat beside me, and I was in the back behind the passenger.

And they get out on which I know now to be the autobahn, and we're sailing along there. I'm looking and the speedometer is up over a hundred. And I thought: Good Lord, you know. I was afraid we were gonna crash. I didn't -- it's kilometers. It wasn't miles per hour.

And they took me to the Dulagluft, which was the Air Force interrogation camp. Now, I knew about the Dulagluft because in our training we were told about Dulagluft that's where they go, and be sure you don't tell them stuff and so forth. Dulagluft was located in the center of Frankfurt in what it's called the Palmengarten. It's a beautiful garden. Been back there since then. No evidence of the camp.

And at this point I have not seen, you know, another American. I don't know what happened to anybody on my, my plane. I'm all alone. And put me in a cell. And it's typical of a, a jail cell -- little window, a bunk and a table in there and not much else as I recall. And they closed the door. And I still got my escape pack. I don't know what I had on it still. Had it, must have had it stuffed in my, my flight suit somehow. So I took it out and I hid it under the mattress. No idea what I thought I'd do with that.

And they took me out and they took pictures. I, I have a copy of this picture. I've got my German record there. And they interviewed me. I don't think they fingerprinted me. But eventually they took me back to the cell, except they put me in a cell next to the one where I'd hid the escape pack.

And I remember later on I knew there was someone over there, and I was trying to communicate back and forth but he couldn't find anything. I, I don't know whether we could, we must have been able to hear each other if we yelled loud enough or something but, but I'm all alone. I don't know who that is over there. And, and every day two, three times a day they'd come in to try to interview you to get information. And if you -- they tried to bribe you with, with, give you a cigarette if you wanted. They'd blow smoke in your face, and they tried to tease you in all kinds of -- we didn't wear our shoes in there. You, you were let out twice a day -- once in the morning and one in the evening.

You were the only person out to go to the toilet. And when you got out, you could see all these shoes sitting out like a motel. You could see these shoes and you know those are British shoes and those are, must be an American in there. You recognize what it was. Never saw anybody.

And after a week, the fellow in frustration says: "All right. You no tell me. I tell you. You're from the 381st Bomb Group stationed in Ridgewell, and everybody got out of your plane except the pilot, and it's believed that he died in the crash." I was in the 381st Bomb Group. They were right on with that. And I, I hope I didn't, you know, say, oh, yes, or, you know, I just listened to that.

And I think it was that same day that they took me and, took me to a room where there were four, five Americans. One of them was the bombardier on my crew. I -- so somebody that I knew. And I, I guess I probably started feeling a little better already. And we were only there for maybe an hour or two and then they released us out into a compound where there were possibly as many as a hundred Americans. And most of my crew was there. And a lot of people that I trained with in Texas that were in the same bomb group that I was with, remember -- what did I say -- four planes from our squadron went down.

We lost planes from our bomb group. One of them crash-landed in, in the channel and got back but ten people. And later, statistics after the war show that on the original crews about 50 -- the people that will got shot down, it was about 50 percent ended up POWs, percent killed. So even though I was a POW, I was lucky.

And from then on I had company. And we were there maybe just a day or two, it seemed to me. I don't -- seemed to me I slept on a table or something there. There was Colonel Spivey got shot down the same day I did. He was the commanding officer of the, some air training command here in the states. He came over to observe flak and he got a good observation his first trip. But he was in the compound on a blanket. And they, they issued me some clothes but the closest they could come was some British shoes that were too big for me. And it was obvious apparently because this colonel -- I was standing near him, and he said: "They're a little big, aren't they, Sergeant?" And I said: "Yes, sir." And he said: "Well, we're gonna have to put up with, with some inconveniences for a while," he said.

Very -- we were taken from -- then we walked to the railroad station, and the only person that rode was this colonel. The, the other officers didn't but they respected his rank. He ended up being the man of confidence or the, the American representing the people in Luft 3 that was an officer's camp, and I think he retired as a general when he finally came back. And we were put in boxcars and that's the method that they used. And you didn't have a, a toilet in a boxcar. You had a, a bucket or something if, if you had to relieve yourself and it was crowded. And you couldn't see what was going on. You just knew you were going and so forth. And I don't remember how long it took but we ended up in -- sometimes you'd sit for a while in a marshalling yard in Kremms (ph), Austria -- or excuse me, in Munich, Germany. And in Munich, we then walked to the Camp Stalag 7A. And we were there for two months.

And we were waiting for them to finish up on a camp in Kremms, Austria. And then we were taken from there again. You, you walked every place. Put you in boxcars again. Took you to Kremms, Austria. Was all Air Force then when we were there, it was, and they were all -- the camp kept receiving people up until March of '44, I think. So most of the people that were prisoners for a long time, Air Force people anyway, were -- enlisted people were in the same camp where I was. The boxcar rides were not fun. I, I generally tell me people that, you know, things were miserable, but I was sharing it with people I knew. Misery loves company and I had both.
(END OF SIDE ONE, TAPE ONE; BEGIN SIDE TWO, TAPE ONE.)

sp.speaker: Maynard Wesley Unger
sp.p: ... first camp because my name is a German name. I was called out a couple times and interviewed to see if I had any relatives in Germany. And again, you know, name, rank and serial number, but I know on my dog tags it gives my parents' name. Well, I, I don't know as I knew for sure, but I assumed that they wanted to use them as a wedge of some sort on my behalf. I didn't have any over there. The name Unger is frequent in Germany. And once in a while we'd see a German paper -- couldn't read it or understand it -- but when the name was written in the obituary or something, why, I'd know who it was.

People often want to know, you know, what, what the conditions were. When we first started out, we had a lot of Red Cross parcels. And as the war went on, transportation became a problem for them to get food to us. So instead of having a, a, maybe a Red Cross parcel every two weeks, why, maybe we would get one, it would be three weeks. Or maybe we would get one and have to share it with somebody. And eventually, of course, it got down to the point where you didn't get Red Cross parcels.

We were permitted to write home. I don't remember. We could write something like two letters and three or four postcards a month. We could receive mail. We could receive packages. I, I can't remember exactly what I got, but I know I was asking to send flour and send stuff because we -- you, you combined with people. You'd have three or four people and whatever I had belonged to you and whatever they had belonged to me. And so you'd try to do everything you could to try to put things together to eat and stay alive. The, the diet has since been proved awhile but a lot of black bread or, and, and it indeed did -- in my records here I do have, it was analyzed it did have some sawdust in it but I suppose sawdust has nourishment the same as other things we eat that didn't, that didn't damage, I don't think it did. But soup, watered-down soup or, or sad soup, imitation soup, potatoes, rutabagas. I don't eat rutabagas, I'll tell you that.

I just -- and I, I've often, you know, when, when you're, when you're hungry, I mean you do and eat most anything. There's a lots of things I won't. I turn my nose up now. Up in my head I don't like 'em. I, I won't even taste 'em.

But I -- two incidents. I know the soup oftentimes had bugs in it. That, that didn't bother you. If you noticed them, you just pushed them out of the way a little bit but it didn't bother you. Another time I remember somebody threw their potato skins away and, boy, they pealed them pretty thin. And I picked them up out of their little trash and put 'em on a, a -- we did have a, a stove of sorts but -- to warm them up and to eat them and so you -- and another time I remember we used to get oleo or margarine in our -- and put that margarine on a piece of bread. And I remember once I dropped it and it landed on the floor of the barracks.

And the floor of the barracks was probably an inch thick with mud, just smooth-packed mud. The only way you could sweep was with these brooms are made out of sticks, you know, they -- but butter side right down. Pick it up and blow it off and say right in that clean piece of paper. We don't do those things today but thing, things were tough in that regard.

I, I don't -- I think the thing that bothered the POW the most was not the harsh living conditions or the, the lack of food. I, I think mostly it's a mentalilty kind of thing. It bothers people in different ways. In, in -- you find people that -- and it isn't just the POW. It's -- soldiers come back and they want to get that out of their mind and they've learned since then that since the Vietnam War that posttraumatic stress syndrome never goes away. And people just keep wanting not talk about something. And the best thing they can do to get it out -- and I'm, I'm going to speak on behalf of the, the American Ex-Prisoner of War organization of which I was, I joined in 1980. I didn't become active until I retired in 1982. I did put a career in the Air Force. I got recalled for the Korean War and then I stayed in. Then I was a school teacher for years, elementary school teacher.

I never once told my kids that I was a POW. My daughter said that: "We never asked you about it because we thought you didn't want to talk about it." I was not aware of that. But I have to tell you that since I've been a member of the POWs, that therapeutic value of being together with people with the same experience where they get acquainted and talk about it, not only did they talk about it, they'd laugh about the terrible things and so forth. Our meetings are a joyous kind of thing. And there's still so many people that haven't even, you know, come out yet.

And the people that come back from Iraq, you know, not only are they seeing all of this shooting and going on, they're doing the shooting. They gotta live with that when they come back. It's gonna be a terrible situation for them. I'm editorializing here.

But we had recreation in camp. We had books, limited stuff from -- some records. We had our own entertainment. We had the cardboard playhouse. They'd put shows on. Some people had been teachers before the war, conducted some classes. People when they came back got college credit. They gave 'em college credit when they came back for the courses that they took over there. And a lot of camaraderie, of course. The, the barracks were cold. The water was only turned on certain hours of the day and it was only cold water. You had to use it to -- you had a spigot that you could get under if you were brave enough.

I remember there was a fella that was -- our barracks had two different ends to 'em, about 150 people in each end. I was in barracks called 39B, but there was a fellow that lived in 39A, and he was like a Charles Atlas, he was, and he'd get under that cold spigot and ice all around on the outside. "Mind over matter," he'd say.

But -- and the food. There was a doctor in our camp who was a, an American major that had been captured in Italy, and he was limited as to what he could do, but there was a, a dispensary there. He had a few things that he could help people with if they got a cold or a slight injury or something. Towards the end of the war, people --

another thing, we didn't -- did you know what was going on? Yes. In our, in our camp there was a radio someplace. I don't know where it was or who had it, but every night there would be somebody who used to work on the radio, would come around. We'd post guards at both of the doors in the barracks. He'd hop up on a table and he'd read the newspaper of the day. We followed the invasion daily where they were going. And from the time the invasion took place, we knew for sure that we were gonna get home.

One particular interest is one day -- and each camp had one person that they elected to be their camp leader, and ours was a staff sergeant. He was not, you know, the ranking person but he was our man of confidence. And he had people that helped him with his connections with all of the eventually our camp had 4,000 people in it. But one day one of these people that worked in -- we called that the White House -- came over to me and said: Sometime in the near future you're gonna get a package from an organization in New York State, and when you get it, we want to see it. I don't remember how long it was but I did indeed get this package. Now, the, the Germans, whenever a package comes in, the Germans open them all up, inspect them. If there's any food that looks like it's got shelf life, they make sure they poke a hole in the can or rip open a bag or something so you couldn't really save things for a big escape or something.

So I called him and he came over and we had my package out, and there was a Ping-Pong set, cribbage set. Those were two things I -- but almost everything in there had something hidden in it, you know -- batteries, wires, money, escape items were in my package. There was another boy from Oberlin that got a package from the same organization just like mine, and I went over to his place and I was gonna show him what he got. He had nothing. I ruined his stuff in his package. They knew that that package was coming to me and it had something in it. Now, this, this is real confidence that Uncle Sam knows where you are. And so I always had that feeling I knew that they, they knew where we were.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Now, his package. What do you mean, his package had none of those items in it?

sp.speaker: Maynard Wesley Unger
sp.p: Had all the same items.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Maynard Wesley Unger
sp.p: But nothing hidden.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Nothing hidden?

sp.speaker: Maynard Wesley Unger
sp.p: Yeah. See, you have to break the Ping-Pong paddle --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: In order to get the stuff, right?

sp.speaker: Maynard Wesley Unger
sp.p: Yeah. It was hidden in it, built right in it. His didn't have any. Before we -- then, when it got down near the end, we were told that we were gonna march out the next day and that we could take anything we want to with us. Well, you know, this was -- we didn't have backpacks like the boy scouts or book packs like the kids do today, what you had was your blanket and, and whatever personal belongings you, you were able to have and you carried 'em as best you could.

And like every younger boy scout, they carried all of this stuff, and after the first mile, why, you could just see stuff thrown all over. I don't remember exactly how far we went but it, it's written down in my book. There's a, a -- somebody kept a diary, but we walked anywheres from 15 to 20, 25 miles a day.

And they just -- you'd sleep in an open field. There was always a stream nearby for maybe -- one time I remember I slept in a, a barn of a house, and it happened to be the day after Roosevelt was, died, because I went to this little house. There were several of us. My one waist gunner was with me. We were always together.

And she was telling us: Roosevelt tot, and we didn't believe her. But that was the day after he had died. This same lady I gave my, my log book, I had a log book in our camp anyway. Most people were given a book, you know, book size full of empty pages, just blank pages. You could put anything in it you wanted to. You could keep a diary. You could draw pictures. You could write poetry. It was yours to keep. I had a lot of stuff in mine. I was afraid he was gonna -- when we got to the end it was gonna be taken away from us.

I bribed this gal into mailing it to me. Never got it. And that was a bad judgment because it would never have been taken away from me. So we were -- on this march, we went from Kremms, Austria, to Braneau (ph), Austria, crisscrossing all along the Danube River, and it wasn't beautiful to us at the time. And people, people that couldn't walk were left at the camp, and of course the Russians came in and got the camp. You could hear the Russians coming. You could hear the firing going off before this happened.

They, they for whatever reason they didn't want the, the Russians to liberate us. We ended up in Braneau, Austria, and there is a big woods. And before we'd gotten there, they had trimmed the trees out in a big square of woods, had a guard tower at each of the four corners and that's where we were. We were just turned loose in there and that's where we were when we were liberated.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Now, when was this move? Was this in '45?

sp.speaker: Maynard Wesley Unger
sp.p: This was 1945.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: In the spring of '45 or something?

sp.speaker: Maynard Wesley Unger
sp.p: April of '45.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right but obviously (inaudible.)

sp.speaker: Maynard Wesley Unger
sp.p: And it was still cold spring. It's, it snowed once while we were walking, and I know it snowed once when we were in the woods, not a heavy, deep snow, but it was cold, you know. You got no protection. We probably ruined the trees in the woods. People make lean-tos and did all kinds of things.

Along the way, we -- one time we went by one of the Nazi concentration camps and prior to us reaching the front of that, there was a group of Jews were being marched in the opposite direction. Looked like walking skeletons coming down, and a few of 'em spoke English, you know: "Help us." We couldn't do anything. If we tried to do something to 'em, they'd take it out on the Jew, not us.

When those people dropped, they'd just killed 'em right on the spot. Kept going. We, we stopped. What I am telling you are some things that, that my, my wife has been with me when I've talked to people that saw the same thing and so, you know, it isn't just made up, but were -- a honey wagon or a horse-drawn, used horses, cattle, anyway a wagon, and it'd come along in the ditches and they'd just pick these bodies up and just throw 'em up in the wagon like they were a sack of wheat or something.

That's the worse thing that I saw in, in all of my -- And we used to try to do bad things to the Germans to irritate 'em if, if we could but, you know, I was not beaten. If you got caught at something or if you got caught trying to escape, you perhaps were punished, but by and large the Germans really tried to uphold the Geneva Convention. They tried to give us what we'd call civil treatment. They just didn't have it to give us. And then --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What were some of the bad things that you did to the Germans to annoy them?

sp.speaker: Maynard Wesley Unger
sp.p: Well, I remember -- I, I was not one that did this but -- I'm not sure how often but every couple months or so they'd take us up to the delouser because, you know, we'd get scabies and, and fleas and get all kinds of lice, and they'd take us up and shave all the hair off of our body -- private parts, your head, everything.

And this one time a few people thought they, they'd put grease in their hand and mix sand in with it and when the clippers went through it, it jammed their clippers up. And I remember this one guard. He just, he just went crazy.

He took his pistol off and, you know, that, that's one of the times when I was really afraid that, for our life that it was gonna happen, but better judgment settled in there somehow. I don't know how that calmed it down. But I really was scared that, that would be one of the things.

We had a Russian in our camp. I don't know where he was. And the Germans would take us out. They were gonna search the barracks and they'd keep us out there. Didn't matter how cold it was. We'd sing and just like we were having a picnic just to irritate the Germans. That's one thing. You can't, you can't beat the morale of the American. He just -- and, of course, we didn't work. We stood roll call twice a day, and if the number was right, you went about your business.

What'd you do? Well, people did a lot of things. Unfortunately, some people just laid on their bunks and sulked, and it's terrible. But we had records. We had recreation. I was not a ballplayer or anything. My ball turret gunner was a boxer. There was a guy out in South Amherst. Whenever he thinks of Blue Pollard, he says: "I lost not money but food on him betting it."

We were the original mall walkers, I think. We walked the compound. Walked the compound. And I played cards. I, I came back thinking I was one of the world's best bridge players. Married a gal who don't play cards. And the -- we were living in this woods, and all of a sudden one day you could here cheering and it was just off in the distance and it got louder and louder and louder, kind of like a wave except once it started, it never stopped and it just, you look and here comes an American Jeep coming along a dirt, dirt highway, driving along the woods, pulled into an area that was up near where I was.

People just got around that like it would be Time Square almost, you know. And this, this -- I was close enough where I could see this captain got out of this Jeep and he looked around, and I, I, I got the feeling he, he couldn't believe what he was seeing really. But he finally said: "You men are no longer prisoners of war but soldiers of the United States Army."

Boy, they could have lifted that Jeep up and the energy that was there. By that time our guards had disappeared. And he said that they were ahead of the troops, you know, maybe as much as two days but they would be along and would take care of us. And I think it was the next day people came in and they started to systematically move us to an abandoned aluminum factory that was in the Town of Kremms. And I don't remember. We were fed, I know that. I don't remember exactly how that was done.

We were only there a couple, three days, and then they took us by GI truck to a small airfield, and C-47s came in and picked us up. I remember two things at the air field. There was a, a German airplane there, one with a fiber cover, not -- like canvas cover, not, not metal -- and it had holes all over but it was a swastika on the side. And just before I got in the plane, somebody threw a, a bayonet down on the ground that they decided they didn't want. I picked it up and I brought that home. I only brought home that bayonet, a watch, and some wings that I'd made while I was over there.

And we went -- and I don't remember the name of the town in France, and we were there and I, I, in my, I don't know, we were sleeping in some little building when the war ended, I know. I was always tempted to write -- you know, they said if you helped eliminate or if you were in France from, from the invasion up until the end of the war, why you could get this French ribbon or whatever it is. Well, I was in France. And I thought -- but I, I'm not big on medals but I felt I qualified.

But then they took us from there, got on trains, nice trains, no boxcar, and we rode up to Camp Lucky Strike, which is in Le Havre, France, and there were all kinds of people and reunions taking place, and they were deprogramming us, interviewed us, and gave us decent clothes to wear and they had USO shows.

And our food -- I, I'd forgotten a letter that I had that was given out to the people there about don't think that we're trying to starve you because that's how they were controlling our diet, our diet. And then I saw my pilot there.

I, I, I thought my pilot was dead up until then. But he'd been on the loose for two weeks. He wasn't killed, and I saw this Buss Beeson, a friend of mine that was with me in basic training, and early on, that washed out. He came up and slapped me on the back and said: "I'd been looking all over Germany for you." He knew I had been a prisoner. And he got shot down during the last month of the war. He ended up getting on B-24s, I think.

And then, of course, the, the big thing is you keep looking at bulletin boards, see when you were gonna ship out. And we got our orders. The boat was the Marine Dragon. And down in the underplace where the bunks were, one wall was painted with a symbol of the 13th Armored Division, and the 13th Armored Division is the division that liberated us. Just ironically it happened to be there. And on the trip back -- during, during the camp, I, I was in one of the shows over there.

Why me, how I got involved, but I did the dance of the seven veils. Of course, you know I was a good looking guy but had these falsies on and a G-string, and they, they wanted me to do this -- the guys that, that rode 17B eventually were organizing some entertainment -- they happened to be on the same boat. And I said: "No, I retired." But we went into New York City, passed the Statue of Liberty and it's -- you just can't describe the, the feeling that, that, that gives a person.
This is where I usually choke up. The good things I choke up on.

They couldn't dock us in New York City. Too many people coming back. So they sent us up to Boston, and we came through Boston because, and that was good fortune obecause my bomb group was coming back from England, and I got to see some of the people that were the ground crew in our bomb crew so that was a nice reunion there. And then, of course, the next -- of course we want to get some money. Got all this money coming to us. And looking for orders home.

And this, this kid, he's, he's a year older than I am. He lives in South Amherst. He's still alive, not really well but he's, he's alive. He was a companion of mine quite a bit in camp. He looked up, up to me like I was his father, I think, but he's older than I am. But we came through Wellington, Ohio. The train does not normally stop there. The train stopped and let us off. And a friend of his family picked us up, drove me to 87 East College Street. And I can hear my dad now. It's him. It's him. And it was just a joyous reunion. And after talking for about a half an hour, what do you think the first thing I wanted to do?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That's a good question.

sp.speaker: Maynard Wesley Unger
sp.p: Probably never guess. I wanted to see if I could drive the car. And so another fella, a friend of mine before the war, lived in Vermillion. Had been injured in the Battle of the Bulge and was a prisoner, was repatriated early. He was home recuperating, and we were some of the early ones back because it was soon after the war.

I got home on Father's Day, so that would have been June of '45, and they hadn't really started to muster people out yet. And he and I spent -- I bought a, a 1940 Hudson convertible from the Smiling Irishman here in Cleveland. I didn't have it very long. I realized why he was smiling.

But we spent just a wonderful time. And he, he had gone to college. He, he'd -- I was home for 60 days. My orders read: Assigned to 87 East College Street for 60 days, and report to Miami, Florida. So we were constant companions for two months. He had been to Indiana University one year before he went in service. And he kept pulling my chain to go to college.

And finally I agreed that I would do it. And he wanted me to go to Indiana. So I went down with him. And my high school transcript was not good enough for an out-of-state student to go to Indiana University. The only way I could get in was to take admission tests. And I said: "We're going home." "No."

He, he talked me into taking the test. I took one of the, one of the tests. There were five of 'em all together. I took one on Friday. And I don't know, I got something like 72. You had to average 70 on whatever it was. And I said: "No. I'll never make it." So I stayed Saturday. I took four more tests, and I averaged exactly 70. They accepted me as a student. And so I signed up, got a room and everything, came home.

And just before school started, I got notified that they had to cancel my room reservations because of so many Indiana people -- and they get preference -- so then I'm not gonna go to college. And he, he said: "Well, come on. You can stay at the fraternity house." He said, "I'll help you look for a place to stay." He convinced me. And I went down and I stayed at the fraternity house so long that I think they felt they had to pledge me to get their money back, you know. But I'd never gone to college had it not been for him and, of course, the G.I. Bill.

And as it turned out over -- it was just a great thing. I went in the insurance business when I came back, sold life insurance. A friend of mine going back to basic training, Tom Chipman, his dad had the Chipman Agency in Columbus. He told me, you know, whenever I got out, and his dad took me on to, to work for Equitable Life of New York. And then I really was too much of a gadabout. I, I didn't like working all those long hours and, and -- but during that period, I'd met my wife. And then, then I got recalled. I got notice for recall for the Korean War.

I was in the reserves. Kind of a humerous thing. When I first met my wife, it was a weekend of the reserve duty, and I was supposed to meet them at 5 o'clock. Well, I learned around 3 o'clock that I was flying to Detroit, and I had a phone number but I was missing a digit and I didn't know which digit I didn't have. I couldn't call her to tell her that I wasn't gonna come. So at 5 o'clock I was on the tarmac at the Detroit Wayne Airport. So I showed up over here as late as 7 o'clock or something like that.

And the people that set this double date up had already gone, and she'd gone up to change clothes and, and finally she agreed to go with me. We went downtown. And it's, it's only one of two times that I ever bumped into anybody in Cleveland that I went to school with. There was a fella -- he wasn't in my fraternity but we bumped into him on the street, went to Clark's Restaurant, and at that time there used to be a lot of cameramen take pictures, just casual, of people on the street and give you a card.

If you wanted to get a picture, you sent a dollar, $2 or whatever it was. The guy took our picture that night, and I've got that picture in my book of our first date. And -- but then when I got recalled, it was for the the 15th of October.

We got married on the 7th, went on a honeymoon, and I shipped off to California -- or Greenville, South Carolina, and subsequent, because of my military service, I was able to, while I was still on active duty, get a master's degree from the University of Southern California. When I was in Germany, they had a graduate school and I was able to attend school and still work and had a good, understanding boss that let me work different hours a little bit.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You were sent to Germany during the Korean War then?

sp.speaker: Maynard Wesley Unger
sp.p: Yeah. I ended up going to Germany. And I was in during the Vietnam War but I didn't -- I was in Germany also during the, during some of it anyway. I spent six years back in Germany so -- and I still don't speak German very well. But I, I found them to be very friendly.

Going back to the Dulagluft, I was in public relations when I was in Germany, and we worked with the press a lot. And this one reporter for the Kaiser Laterne newspaper told me he was a translator at Dulagluft. What he really was was an interrogator probably, but he was a nice guy. And he gave me one of the road signs that sat along the road directing people to Dulagluft. It was a nice, thick wooden sign, hand-painted German logo. He gave me that. And I have since turned that over to the Air Force Museum down at Wright-Pat. And it's kind of an historic document. Every -- I think probably almost without exception almost every air crew member -- officer, enlisted -- went through Dulagluft.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Were there any other memorable missions in those first 12 before you were shot down?

sp.speaker: Maynard Wesley Unger
sp.p: Well, I, I -- we, we got not shot up badly, but on one of our missions we were, our raft, our lifesaving raft got loose. I suppose it, something triggered it, and it hung up on the stabilizer. So you got the stabilizer and here's this raft on it. And there was a, a chance that we might have to bail out but the pilot was able to, to keep it under control and figured it was safe so -- we always joked about it if we got shot down, we were always gonna head for Switzerland.

I wouldn't have had any direction, any idea what direction Switzerland was when I went down and -- 'cause I, I was really scared. Once my, my electric suit had a short in it someplace and I got frostbite on my fingers and on my toes, and there's always a question whether that happened, whether when I was a POW, because a lot of people got frostbite. But I, I'm pretty sure my fingers did then.

I, I don't -- the sad things, you know, when you see a plane go down and you know the people that are on it, pretty generally when you see all that, it's a generic, you know, it's -- you don't know but when it's someone that you know like that's their plane, that, that's really hard.

And up until the time that we went down, our little squadron was pretty good but they took the lump all at once. And they, they recognized people. I was given my air medal over there in cermonies. My father was given an air medal at cermonies held at -- which was then Fenn College. In the picture, he's holding the box, so I don't know whether -- I've only got one air medal, whether that's the one -- but it was kind of a, in my opinion a publicity to let people know there were four people, four parents receiving air medals.

One of them was a radio operator in our squadron, in addition to me. His name was Kearn. And, of course, we were missing in action at that time. But Kearn, he was killed. And when there's a newspaper -- I, I had the good fortune of, I knew a lot of people at the newspaper before I went in the service, and good friends, a sports writer, and the papers just had a lot of stuff when I went in the service, when I completed basic training, when I went overseas, when I got shot down, POW liberated, all of that.

But when I got shot down, there was an article in there. It is believed that I'm still alive because a fellow from my, that knew me from my squadron -- I can't -- he came back and was a barber, had some kind of, I don't know whether he just wrote or had a code to his wife or what -- but he wrote and said that he saw me go down in a parachute and that, that I was alive. I don't know how he could do that. I don't know how he knew it was me. You rec -- all you see is a blurp of someone going.

But anyway, maybe he saw a lot of chutes. Maybe he counted all of them. Now, that's possible. I know I didn't. But that he knew that I was alive. They knew. They had this information before they were officially notified that I was missing in action.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Maynard Wesley Unger
sp.p: They knew that I'd been shot down. They were on vacation in Ruggles Beach. And what else can I tell you?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I don't know. You think that covers it?

sp.speaker: Maynard Wesley Unger
sp.p: I, I just -- I have to remark that I think that my POW experience made me a better person. I can't put my finger on any one thing 'cause I don't know how I would have turned out without it but it definitely -- and ever since then I've been blessed with some kind of a leadership ability, which in different things that I've been involved with always seems, I think it, it might be because I can't keep my mouth shut or, you know, I -- people get to know who I am or something.

But I -- my tail gunner -- two things I'd like to tell you about my tail gunner, which one of 'em is, very definitely has to do with this. I visited him in 1950. I was in, on business in Philadelphia, looked in the phone book and Joseph R. Lyons was in there. And I called him, and he said: "I'll come down to the hotel" -- he arranged for a time -- "bring you out for dinner." He came down. He picked me up. His wife was in the kitchen doing the final things. He and I are seated at the table, and he kind of turned to me and he said: "You know, I'm Jewish."

And it was almost like "I got that off my shoulders." He, he said he always felt bad that he kept that a secret, but he said at one of our sessions way back in Texas, he said that Colonel Nazaro (ph), who was our commander, said: "Now, you Jewish boy" -- I'm just paraphrasing -- "you Jewish boys might want to think twice about leaving your religion on your dog tags, because one of two things will probably happen to you. You'll either get shot down, become a POW, or get killed."

And he had it taken off his dog tags. Nobody on the crew knew that he was Jewish. And it was almost like "boy, I'm glad I, I" -- like it bothered him for years. I ended up spending -- after I got recalled -- 26 and-a-half years in the service. I would never -- I got a master's degree.

I would have never gone to college. I didn't even know what college was when I got out of high school. Never even thought of going. It gave me a wonderful career. It led me into the second career of teaching. If I'd written down a hundred things that I'd like to do when I -- as a career, teaching probably would never have been one of 'em, but it was a wonderful, wonderful opportunity for me and, of course, I have also -- maybe I got into teaching because a, a man convinced me to do that because I was so successful working with kids in the boy scouts so I've been blessed many ways. My family and my wife and the Veterans Administration in recent years has taken a new look at the POW.

Two things happened in -- recently . I don't know who's listening to this -- but the Iraqi war -- we had four, five people taken prisoner for a matter of just a few days. And up until -- well, still, you have to have been a POW for 30 days to qualify for benefits. Secretary of Veterans Affair, Anthony Principi, says that may have been the case years ago for lack of food and, and living conditions and so forth, but today we need to take another look at that because even a prisoner for a few days does something to the individual. So I look for them to change that and reward those people as such.

But they realize the Vietnam War brought about a lot of counseling that was not there when we first came home, and this has helped a lot of people. There are many people that attend -- regular members in our POW group that still regularly attend these, at rap sessions with the VA, and I'm real thankful for that. They seem to be fine. But in certain cases they just break down uncontrollable crying and so forth. And I thank you, Tom Swope, for asking me to be interviewed, and I think it's a wonderful program and it will help somebody. Somebody might find one or two things that they didn't know. Thanks again.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Thank you.
(END OF INTERVIEW)
